video.title: He Makes $3M/Year From Tiny AI Tools (Here’s How You Can Too)

summary: John Rush describes building a portfolio of small software products and AI agents, with SEO Bot as a standout product and the portfolio generating around 3 million a year in combined revenue. He explains how he develops tools for his own use, validates demand before building, and grows products through SEO, social content, partnerships, directories, and cross-selling. The discussion also covers internal-first agents, niche directories, and example tools such as a listing bot and analytics product. The key takeaway is to find a real problem, test whether the right customers will pay, and automate recurring work gradually while keeping useful human checks.

speakers.name: John Rush
speakers.description: Founder building a portfolio of software products and AI agents.

ideas.name: Portfolio of small software products and AI agents
ideas.one_liner: Build small software tools for internal use, validate them with friends and prospective users, then release and grow the ones that work.
ideas.business_model: Multiple software products with subscriptions and other product-specific pricing; customers can move between products in the portfolio.
ideas.customer: Busy founders and other users of the individual tools; specific customers vary by product.
ideas.problem: Small, specific work problems are underserved by larger companies, while founders want tools that reduce repetitive work and run with limited oversight.
ideas.offer: A portfolio of small web products and agents, first built and used internally, then shared with friends and eventually launched publicly.

pricing.model: Product-specific; recurring subscriptions are mentioned, along with one-off pricing for some products.
pricing.notes: Portfolio-wide pricing was not stated. The transcript mentions product-specific prices elsewhere.

acquisition_channels.details: Starts SEO work early on products and uses articles, tools, backlinks, directories, and search demand to attract users.
Uses social content to reach people beyond existing followers and to prompt mentions, links, and recommendations.
Sets up partner links and commissions so others can promote products.
Places products in directories, launchpads, forums, Reddit, Quora, and other relevant places.
Friends and early users can share pre-launch pages with others who want the product.

ideas.delivery: Web-based software and agents. John says he builds and operates products himself, initially using them internally; agents do recurring work and can ask him for decisions when uncertain.
unit_economics_claims: The projects together generate around 3 million a year in revenue; currency was not stated.
Three products generate most portfolio revenue.
Cross-selling between products accounts for about half of new-user sales in some months.

acquisition.how: SEO publishing, referral links, and scheduled content can be automated, but product positioning, partnership work, and channel choices need human judgment. Cold direct messages described in the transcript need UK consent and privacy checks.

onboarding.how: Software sign-up and trials can be automated; product-specific setup and edge cases may still need a person.

delivery.how: The products are software and agents that perform recurring work, with the operator asked for decisions when the agent lacks confidence.

billing.how: Subscriptions and online payments can be handled by software, though the transcript does not detail the billing setup.

support.how: Agents can request human input and report progress, but the operator describes handling accounting and user feedback himself.

uk_applicability.notes: The model is web software and can serve UK customers. The product niches and prices may need local adjustment.

risks: A large portfolio can create support and legacy-maintenance work; John says he limits customer counts to keep support manageable.
Search rankings and SEO results can change over time.
Cold DMs or marketing emails to UK individuals and sole traders require consent under PECR; cold email rules differ for limited companies.
Automating work without enough human review can lead to poor output or a product that does not meet customer needs.

tactics.name: Build from a problem you experience yourself
steps: Notice a repetitive or frustrating task in your own work.
Build the smallest tool that solves it for you.
Use it yourself long enough to learn its weaknesses before offering it to others.

quote.text: The best ideas are the ideas that scratch your own itch. So, basically, you're doing a job and then you have a problem at the job
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Validate search demand before building
steps: Use Google autocomplete to find how people complete a query such as “website builder for”.
List roughly 50 to 60 candidate ideas in a spreadsheet.
Check keyword volume and competition, then compare related phrases for the same audience.
Use the results to decide whether a niche has enough demand and a reachable audience.

quote.text: I usually play with it for an hour. I make a list in the Excel for like 50 or 60 ideas and then I bring them back into the keyword research tool
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Try to disprove the idea
steps: Look for evidence that the idea should not be built.
Check whether search demand comes from the intended buyers.
Test one idea at a time and stop spending build time when the evidence is weak.

quote.text: So basically when I build something I'm trying to convince myself that I shouldn't build it
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Use a waitlist as an early demand test
steps: Build a simple landing page with a clear description and a name-and-email sign-up.
Show it to people in the target audience and track sign-ups.
Use the waitlist to learn whether people will take a small step toward the product, not as proof that they will buy.

quote.text: So now I have my landing page. Show it to potential customers and see normally don't want to join weight lists because it's silly, right?
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Ask for pre-orders to check willingness to pay
steps: Offer a pre-booking at a discount before building the full product.
Track how many waitlist users pay, not just how many sign up.
Ask users who decline whether the issue is price, recurring billing, or the audience being wrong.

quote.text: I give people 70% or 90% discount if they buy now. And surprisingly I had cases where a lot of people signed up for a tool
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Keep a conversation with prospective customers
steps: Collect sign-ups through a waitlist and follow up by email.
Ask for a pre-booking and invite a reply if the price or billing model does not fit.
Use the replies to distinguish a pricing issue from a customer-selection problem.

quote.text: if you get them into your weight And then after a while you send them the payment then you're sending it through the email. So you have the the thread on the email with them
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Start SEO early on products with a long runway
steps: Publish SEO content while developing the product if time allows.
Return after a few months to compare which pages receive traffic.
Use page-level traffic as another signal of whether a niche can be reached.

quote.text: In my case, since I have so many products and they're all not pressing me on on time like I have all all the time in the world, I usually start SEO work on a day one.
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Use social media to earn indirect distribution
steps: Publish useful content that can reach people beyond existing followers.
Look for mentions, blog posts, newsletters, directories, and backlinks that result from the attention.
Continue social posting if the founder has a repeatable way to create content that the niche responds to.

quote.text: Social media is the best way to grow for small products. Right now the best part about social media is that it's not just the people you bring directly from social media
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Offer generous affiliate commissions
steps: Set up an affiliate portal where partners can get unique links and codes.
Use a high commission when product costs allow it.
Give partners a simple way to promote the product and earn from referred customers.

quote.text: You should be really really generous on the commission. Like a lot of people have this like 10% or 15%. You should be crazy generous.
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Seed products where their audience already looks
steps: List relevant directories, launchpads, forums, Reddit threads, and Quora discussions.
Share the product where it directly answers a relevant conversation.
Treat this as both customer discovery and a way to improve the chance that search and AI systems encounter the product.

quote.text: There has to be everywhere on directories, launchpads, forums, Reddits and social media.
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Use a free tool to introduce a paid product
steps: Build a small free tool for a search query that the target customer cares about.
Offer the output through a clear sign-up flow.
Use the delivery message to mention a related paid product.

quote.text: And they would go there, they would generate their album, they would enter their email to receive the PNG in a good quality.
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Build an agent for yourself before selling it
steps: Run the agent internally and use it on real work.
Let it ask questions when it is uncertain and provide feedback.
Release it to friends and then the public once it is stable and the operator understands its limitations.

quote.text: they all start as my internal agent and I run them for a long while so that I'm happy with them myself
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Design billing around the value customers perceive
steps: Ask whether customers see the work as a one-time service or continuing value.
If they reject recurring billing, test one-off pricing.
If they reject a large lifetime payment, test a lower monthly option.

quote.text: people said that why should I pay every month? You just kind of do the work once for me and that's it.
quote.speaker: John Rush

tactics.name: Cross-sell products across a portfolio
steps: Make related products easy to find from each other.
Offer a relevant next tool after a customer has tried one product.
Track whether existing users move into other products and remain in the product ecosystem.

quote.text: when I land one user in any of my tool, like I have some tools that are making like 1K a month, like very small tools
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Start with a problem you experience yourself, then use the product enough to understand its real strengths and weaknesses.

quote.text: The best ideas are the ideas that scratch your own itch.
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Test demand with search data, but check whether the people searching are the same people who would buy.

quote.text: you have to also validate with a product is not just if people want it but also if you're able to drive traffic there
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Try to disprove an idea before spending substantial time building it.

quote.text: you should try to kill your idea because there are so many ideas.
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Waitlist sign-ups indicate interest, but asking for payment is a stronger test of demand and audience fit.

quote.text: if you ask for a payment and you don't get at least 10% of your weight list to, you know, execute it
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Ask prospective customers what feels wrong about price or billing rather than guessing from a failed purchase.

quote.text: if you do this like like imagine if I purchase my payment link like everybody else does then if people don't want it they just leave you have no idea why they don't want it
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Treat SEO as a compounding channel and start early when the product can wait for results.

quote.text: you know after a year you think you should have done a year ago and so it's compounding and you should do it as early as possible
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Make the agent useful to busy customers by having it do the work and ask for judgment only when needed.

quote.text: the end goal for every agent is that I turn it on and I live it and it just works as great employee that self-managed agentic and it asks me whenever it has questions
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Build and test an agent internally before exposing it to a large customer base.

quote.text: they all start as my internal agent and I run them for a long while so that I'm happy with them myself
quote.speaker: John Rush

lessons.lesson: Choose a billing model that matches how often customers believe the product provides value.

quote.text: you just kind of do the work once for me and that's it.

quote.text: I send the data every week on what has been done and maybe there's some views because you don't get clicks right away
